rows.title: The universe and the solar system - origin theories, the Sun, planets, asteroids, comets, meteors
sub: Group-II S2-1: The Earth in our solar system - the Sun, planets and the origin of the earth

secs.t: Universe and solar system — definitions, ages, units and FIRSTs — Definitions and ages

x: The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old, whereas the Earth and the solar system are approximately 4.6 billion years old.
Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, followed by helium.
Rocky planets formed mainly in the hot inner disc, while the cool outer disc retained volatile ices associated with giant planets.
An Astronomical Unit is smaller than a light-year, and a parsec is approximately 3.26 light-years.

secs.t: Universe and solar system — definitions, ages, units and FIRSTs — Types of planets and dwarf planets

x: Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930; it is the largest known Kuiper Belt object and lies at approximately 39 AU.
The discovery of
Eris
, along with the need for a clearer planetary definition, helped prompt Pluto's reclassification as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Mangalyaan is the Mars orbiter, Aditya-L1 is the solar observatory, Aryabhata was the first Indian satellite, and SMILE studies the solar wind-magnetic shield interaction.

secs.t: Scientists → theories and contributions

x: The Nebular hypothesis dates to 1755, the Planetesimal hypothesis to 1904, the Big Bang theory to 1927, and the Steady State theory to 1948.
Georges Lemaitre
proposed the Big Bang theory, also described as the expanding universe theory.
Red-shift (Hubble, 1929) shows expansion and the CMB is the leftover Big Bang glow.

secs.t: Stars and galaxies — life cycle and terms → meaning

x: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with a rotating disc, central bulge and a halo containing dark matter.
Indian researchers identified the spiral galaxy Alaknanda using the
James Webb Space Telescope
(JWST).
A massive star evolves into a supergiant, undergoes a supernova explosion, and may end as a neutron star or black hole.
Polaris is in Ursa Minor, lies close to the north celestial pole, and stars twinkle more noticeably than planets.

secs.t: The Sun — size, layers and solar activity

x: The
core
is the region where hydrogen nuclei undergo nuclear fusion to form helium, at a temperature of approximately 15 million °C.
The photosphere has a temperature of approximately 5,500–6,000°C, while the corona can exceed one million °C. Thus, the corona is hotter than the visible surface despite being farther out.
Solar flares and coronal mass ejections can cause geomagnetic storms and auroras and can disrupt or damage satellites, communication, navigation and power-grid systems.

secs.t: Planets → superlatives and features

x: Exam angle: "no natural satellite", "retrograde rotation" and "least dense" are the most repeated one-liners.
Mercury
remains closest to Earth for the longest time on average because its small orbit keeps it relatively near the other planets.
Mercury
has the largest day-night temperature gap, exceeding 1000°F, because of its slow rotation and very thin atmosphere.
Venus
is the hottest planet, about 464°C on average, because its thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat.
Neptune is not the smallest planet; it is the coldest on average and the farthest planet since 2006, with the longest year (~165 years).
Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium, while methane gives Uranus and Neptune their blue-green tints.

secs.t: Moons → planet → feature

x: The announcement added four moons to Jupiter and eleven moons to Saturn.
Titan is Saturn's moon with a dense atmosphere and ~100 m deep methane lakes.
Ganymede is larger than Mercury, Europa has a subsurface ocean beneath ice, and Charon is Pluto's largest moon.

secs.t: Asteroids, comets and meteors — places and terms → meaning

x: Asteroids are predominantly rocky bodies, while comets contain substantial frozen material and may develop a coma and tail near the Sun.
Solar heating develops the tail near the Sun, and solar radiation and wind cause it to point away from the Sun; comets originate from the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud.
The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, consists of rocky leftovers of the early solar system, and Ceres is its largest body.

secs.t: Orbit terms → meaning

x: Perigee is the Moon's nearest approach to Earth; a full Moon at perigee is called a
supermoon
and produces higher tides.
Perihelion ~3 Jan (~147 million km), aphelion ~4 July (~152 million km).
A
blue micromoon
is the second full Moon of a month occurring at apogee.

secs.t: Space missions → target and achievement

x: OSIRIS-REx returned Bennu samples, DART impacted Dimorphos, Hera surveys the Didymos-Dimorphos system, and Hayabusa2 obtained samples from Ryugu.
Aditya-L1 is India's first solar observatory and operates in a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point.
L4 and L5 are stable Lagrange points, while L1, L2 and L3 are unstable.
PSLV-C25 launch in Nov 2013 and Mars orbit on 24 Sep 2014.

secs.t: Earth's unique features — habitability and evolution of the spheres

x: Planetary
differentiation
separated materials according to density, with heavy iron forming the core and lighter material forming the crust.
The early hydrogen-helium atmosphere was lost to the solar wind; interior degassing followed, producing water vapour, nitrogen and carbon dioxide, and photosynthesis later added oxygen.
The geodynamo generated by churning liquid iron in the outer core produces Earth's magnetic field, which shields the planet from the solar wind.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Halo orbit at L1 (~1.5 million km) and decoding of the Oct 2024 storm's compression of the magnetic field.
SMILE will image the solar wind interaction with Earth's magnetic shield using X-ray and ultraviolet observations together.
Sriharikota's SDSC-SHAR launched Aditya-L1 on PSLV-C57 in 2023 and completed its 100th launch on 29 January 2025.

rows.title: Earth - shape, size, geoid; latitudes and longitudes, the graticule

secs.t: Shape of the Earth — terms, evidences and changes

x: The sequence of visibility of an approaching ship, the circular lunar-eclipse shadow, circumnavigation and satellite imagery all support the spherical nature of the Earth.
Melting ice redistributes mass towards the Equator, enhances the equatorial bulge, slows rotation and lengthens the day by about 1.33 milliseconds per century.
The
Survey of India
is building a Geoid Model for the whole country to support precise GPS/GNSS-based height determination.

secs.t: Data — dimensions of the Earth

x: The equatorial diameter is about 12,756 km, the polar diameter about 12,714 km, their difference is about 43 km, and the mean radius is approximately 6,371 km.
The surface area of the Earth is approximately
510 million square kilometres
The Earth's equatorial circumference is about
('nearly 40,000 km').

secs.t: Graticule — terms, counts, distances and traps

x: The intersection of the Equator and the Prime Meridian, represented by 0° latitude and 0° longitude, lies in the
Gulf of Guinea in the Atlantic Ocean
The distance represented by one degree of longitude decreases towards the poles because meridians converge: it is about 111 km at the Equator, 55.5 km at 60° and zero at the poles.

secs.t: Conferences, cartographers and resolutions → meridian and maps

x: The Prime Meridian passing through Greenwich was fixed at the International Meridian Conference in 1884.
The Mercator projection was developed by Gerardus Mercator in 1569.
The African Union backed 'Correct the Map'.

secs.t: Key parallels and meridians → countries crossed

x: The Prime Meridian passes through the United Kingdom, France, Spain, Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo and Ghana.
The Arctic Circle lies at approximately 66°33' N and the Antarctic Circle at approximately 66°33' S. They mark the approximate limits of polar day and polar night.
The Tropic of Cancer crosses 8 States (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram) and cuts the Mahi river twice.

secs.t: Places — city latitudes and India's extreme points

x: The correct north-to-south order is Srinagar, Bhopal, Visakhapatnam and Chennai.
Kibithu in Arunachal Pradesh is the most eastward location, while Guhar Moti in Gujarat is the most westward location.
Rome
is at about 41.9°N, north of New York (40.7°N), Beijing (39.9°N) and New Delhi (28.6°N).
Indira Col in the Karakoram is the northern extreme of India.

secs.t: India and Andhra Pradesh — extent, area, coast and borders

x: Andhra Pradesh extends approximately from 12°41′N to 19°07′N latitude and from 77°E to 84°40′E longitude.
India has an area of approximately 32,87,263 square kilometres, ranks seventh in area, and measures about 3,214 km north-south and 2,933 km east-west.
Chhattisgarh and Odisha lie to the north, Telangana to the west and north-west, Karnataka to the south-west, and Tamil Nadu to the south.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: EOS-05 is described as India's first Earth-imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit, at approximately 36,000 km, allowing frequent observation of the same area.
Andhra Pradesh lies wholly between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer and is described as having a tropical Aw climate.
Kakinada
district hosts the meridian associated with Indian Standard Time.

rows.title: Motions of the earth - rotation and revolution; effects (day and night, Coriolis force, tides)

secs.t: Rotation — direction, period, speed and data

x: Redistribution of mass towards the Equator increases moment of inertia and slightly slows Earth's rotation, lengthening the day by about 1.33 milliseconds per century.
A sidereal day, measured relative to a distant star, lasts 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds.
The constant Earth-Sun distance is not an evidence of Earth's rotation; in fact, the distance varies slightly because Earth's orbit is elliptical.

secs.t: Persons and laws → evidence of the motions

x: In Foucault's 1851 experiment at Paris, the plane of swing of the pendulum slowly turned, providing visible evidence of Earth's rotation.

secs.t: Day and night — terms → meaning

x: The circle of illumination (terminator) divides day from night and is also called the grey line or twilight zone.
The
midnight sun
refers to continuous daylight for 24 hours or more in high-latitude regions during their summer.
Twilight is the period of
diffused light before sunrise and after sunset
, when the Sun is below or near the horizon.

secs.t: Effects of rotation — Coriolis force, polar flattening and tides

x: The Coriolis force (2Ωv sin latitude) is zero at the Equator, maximum at the poles and grows with wind velocity.
As the Earth rotates, a place generally passes through two tidal bulges, producing two high tides and two low tides, with successive similar tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.

secs.t: Revolution — data and leap year

x: The Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, with the Sun located at one of the two foci of the ellipse.
The Sun's gravitational attraction acts as the centripetal force that keeps the Earth revolving around it.
The accumulated extra quarter day produces a leap year with 29 February approximately every four years, with exceptions for century years.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Cyclone movement is influenced by steering winds and broader atmospheric circulation, while the Coriolis effect influences its deflection and rotation.

rows.title: Concept of time - local and standard time, GMT/UTC, Indian Standard Time, time zones, International Date Line
sub: Group-II S2-2: Motions of the earth, latitudes and longitudes, local and standard time, IDL

secs.t: Time — units and terms → meaning (GMT, UTC, DST)

x: A day is related to Earth’s rotation, a month to the Moon’s revolution and a year to Earth’s revolution.
The Prime Meridian through the Royal Observatory, Greenwich was adopted at the International Meridian Conference of 1884.
Daylight Saving Time is intended to make better use of available evening daylight in summer.

secs.t: Local time — rules and worked examples

x: Thirty degrees correspond to two hours, and a place west of Greenwich is behind Greenwich Mean Time.
The journey takes three hours and the eastward movement adds one hour because 15° equals one hour.
The places are on opposite sides of Greenwich, so the degrees are added: 60° + 90° = 150°; 150 x 4 min = 600 min = 10 hours.

secs.t: Time zones → countries

x: The theoretical system divides 360° of longitude into 24 time zones, each 15° wide.
France
has 12 time zones when its overseas territories are included, while Russia has 11.
China
uses one official time zone throughout the country despite its large longitudinal span.
Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and
Colombo
observe UTC+5:30.

secs.t: International Date Line — course, places and crossing rule

x: Big Diomede belongs to Russia and Little Diomede belongs to the United States; they lie close to each other in the Bering Strait but on different calendar dates.
Samoa shifted to the Asian side of the International Date Line in 2011, thereby changing its calendar relationship with nearby countries.
Kiribati’s Line Islands
use UTC+14 and are among the first inhabited places to enter a new day.

secs.t: Indian Standard Time — meridian, reference town, states crossed

x: Mirzapur
in Uttar Pradesh is the reference town associated with the Indian Standard Time meridian.
The meridian crosses
Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
The IST meridian is 82 degrees 30' E (82.5 E).
West Bengal is not crossed by the Indian Standard Time meridian.

secs.t: Institutions, rules and networks keeping IST

x: Separate Bombay and Calcutta times date from 1884, a single IST was adopted after 1947, the White Rabbit network was inaugurated in July 2026, and the Rules were notified on 27 August 2026.
It was inaugurated at RRSL Jakkur, Bengaluru and gives sub-nanosecond sync over fibre, cutting dependence on GPS.

secs.t: Tropic of Cancer → Indian states, cities, meeting point

x: Exam angle: "how many states" (8), "which state is NOT crossed" (Odisha, UP and Bihar are common distractors).
The intersection of the 82°30'E meridian and the Tropic of Cancer occurs in
Chhattisgarh
The Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 States: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.

secs.t: Revolution — solstices, equinoxes and day length (data)

x: Exam angle: APPSC matched winter solstice with 22 Dec, summer with 21 Jun, vernal with 21 Mar, autumnal with Sep 23. It has also accepted "20 or 21 March" and "22 or 23 September" as equinox dates.
Seasons result mainly from the tilt of Earth’s axis combined with Earth’s revolution around the Sun, which changes the angle and duration of solar illumination.
During southern summer, the
South Pole
is tilted towards the Sun, producing longer days and summer conditions in the Southern Hemisphere.

secs.t: Axial tilt and inclination — terms, consequences and changes

x: The Earth's axis is tilted
from the perpendicular to the orbital plane.
Axial tilt is responsible for seasons and unequal day length, and it determines the positions of both the tropics and polar circles.
The Earth's axis slowly wobbles, changing the direction of the celestial pole.
Long-period variations in Earth's orbit and axial behaviour that influence climate are called
Milankovitch cycles

secs.t: Debates — the two-time-zone question

x: The longitudinal span is approximately 29°, which corresponds to about 116 minutes, or nearly two hours.
The north-east experiences sunrise considerably earlier than western India, creating the basis for the separate-time-zone debate.
The debate has included advancing IST by 30 minutes, creating a north-eastern zone about one hour ahead, and retaining 82°30'E as the reference for the national time system.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The IST meridian at 82.5° E passes through five Indian States, including Andhra Pradesh.
The White Rabbit IST network enables synchronised IST time-stamps for banking, digital payments, railways, airports, power grids and telecom, and helps protect against GPS spoofing.
The wide east-west extent creates a daylight disadvantage in the north-east.

rows.title: Seasons - inclination of the axis, solstices and equinoxes, distribution of insolation

secs.t: Causes of seasons — key reason, terms and traps

x: Seasonal variation results from the Earth’s axial inclination, the parallelism of its axis, its revolution around the Sun and its spherical shape.
A hemisphere tilted towards the Sun receives more direct insolation and longer daylight, producing summer conditions.
The Earth is nearest to the Sun around 3 January, during Northern Hemisphere winter.

secs.t: Insolation — factors and distribution

x: Direction of ocean tides
is not one of them.
Insolation generally decreases from the tropics to the poles.

secs.t: Seasons by hemisphere and latitude zone → features

x: Seasonal differences are greatest in
high latitudes
because the annual swings in day length and insolation are very large there.
Low latitudes commonly have wet and dry seasons, subtropical regions have hot summers and mild winters, and mid-latitudes show four distinct seasons.
The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day around 21 June, while the Southern Hemisphere has its longest day around 22 December.

secs.t: Places in India → overhead Sun, day length, hot season

x: Only places between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn can receive the overhead Sun.
On 21 June, the Sun is overhead at
the Tropic of Cancer
, so an object there casts no shadow at local noon.
The hot weather season is March-May, and ~50 degrees C was recorded at Ganganagar (1935).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: AP's summer is March-May, winter October-February, and the SW monsoon (June-September) gives ~2/3 of its rain.
The IMD identifies four seasons: winter, pre-monsoon, South-West monsoon and post-monsoon.
The theme associated with the International Day of Yoga in 2026 is “
Yoga for Healthy Ageing

rows.title: Interior of the earth - crust, mantle, core; discontinuities and seismic evidence
sub: Group-II S2-3: Interior of the earth - crust, mantle, core and the discontinuities

secs.t: Sources of information on the interior — types and places

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2017 - "surface rock from mining areas" is the only direct source among seismic, gravity and magnetic options.
Seismic waves
are an indirect source because their behaviour reveals the structure and properties of inaccessible interior layers.
Meteorites and gravity anomalies are indirect sources, while magma and lava brought out by volcanic eruptions are direct evidence.

secs.t: Persons and institutions → contributions

x: The
Borehole Geophysics Research Laboratory
at Karad conducts scientific deep drilling in India.
Swarm satellite observations indicated a shift beneath the Pacific from sluggish westward flow to strong eastward flow, followed by weakening around 2020.

secs.t: Seismic waves — types, terms and shadow zone

x: Since S-waves cannot travel through
liquid
s and vanish on reaching the outer core, the outer core is inferred to be liquid.
Changes in density alter seismic-wave velocity and produce reflection and refraction at boundaries, revealing internal discontinuities.
The P-wave shadow zone is the belt approximately 105°–145° from the epicentre where direct P-waves are not recorded.

secs.t: Layers — thickness, density and state (data)

x: Oceanic crust is approximately 5 km thick, whereas continental crust is approximately 30 km thick, though it may reach greater thickness beneath mountains.
Continental crust is associated with granitic SIAL, whereas oceanic crust is associated with basaltic SIMA.
The inner core is solid, extends from approximately 5,150 to 6,371 km depth and has a density of about 13.3–13.6 g/cm³.

secs.t: Discontinuities → layers separated

x: The Gutenberg Discontinuity, separating the mantle and core, occurs at approximately
depth.
The Lehmann Discontinuity separates the outer and inner core at approximately
depth.
The Moho separates crust and mantle, varies in depth beneath continents and oceans, and was identified by Andrija Mohorovicic in 1909.
A distinctive increase in P-wave velocity from about
6.9 to 8.1 km/s
helped identify the Moho.

secs.t: Lithosphere and asthenosphere — terms → meaning

x: The asthenosphere is a weak, plastic and partly molten upper-mantle zone, generally associated with depths of 100–200 km, and is a major source of magma.
The dense lower layer of the Indian plate is reported to be peeling away and delaminating into the mantle at roughly 100 km depth beneath Tibet.

secs.t: Composition — SIAL, SIMA, NIFE and crustal elements

x: Exam angle: "Nickel and Ferrum" as the core's main elements; "Silicon" as the extra constituent.
Oxygen is the most abundant element by weight in the crust, followed by
silicon
at approximately 27.72%.
Aluminium
(about 8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust, followed by iron (about 5%) and calcium (about 3.6%).
The core is mainly iron and nickel (NIFE), with lighter elements such as
silicon
, sulphur and oxygen.

secs.t: Core and magnetic field — features

x: Convection of molten iron in the outer core produces dynamo action, which generates Earth's magnetic field.
The Earth's magnetic axis is inclined approximately
to its geographic axis.
All four statements correctly describe the depth ranges and physical states of the outer and inner core.

secs.t: Temperature, pressure and density — gradients and geothermal places

x: Temperature, pressure and density all generally rise with increasing depth inside the Earth.
Temperature rises by approximately 1°C for every 32 m of depth in the upper crust, although the rate slows at greater depths.
The immense pressure caused by the weight of overlying material keeps the inner core solid despite its extreme temperature.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The global mapping referred to mantle earthquakes occurring more than 80 km below the Moho; their surface shaking is generally weak.
Diamonds formed in the mantle are transported upward to the crust through
kimberlite pipes
The magnetic field generated by the liquid outer core helps shield life from the solar wind and cosmic radiation.

rows.title: Rocks and minerals - igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic; the rock cycle
sub: Group-II S2-4: Rocks - igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic; the rock cycle

secs.t: Composition of the Earth — crustal elements by rank (data)

x: Exam angle: "most abundant metal" = aluminium, not iron; "most abundant element" = oxygen; whole-Earth question = iron.
Oxygen
is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust, constituting approximately 46.6% by weight.
SIAL has a density of about 2.9, SIMA is basaltic and associated with magma, and NIFE forms the nickel-iron core with a density of about 11.

secs.t: Minerals → class, order of crystallisation, hardness

x: Muscovite is a phyllosilicate, albite is a tectosilicate, hornblende is a double-chain inosilicate and augite is a single-chain inosilicate.
The first four minerals on the Mohs scale are talc, gypsum, calcite and fluorite, with hardness values from 1 to 4 respectively.
Quartz is silicon dioxide (SiO2), is relatively hard and resistant to weathering, and is a major component of granite and sandstone.

secs.t: Rock types → examples; igneous rocks

x: Marble, slate and quartzite are metamorphic rocks, whereas
limestone
is a sedimentary rock and a parent rock of marble.
Slow cooling within the crust permits the growth of large crystals, as seen in granite and gabbro.
Granite is felsic intrusive, rhyolite is felsic extrusive, diorite is intermediate intrusive and basalt is mafic extrusive.

secs.t: Sedimentary rocks — modes of formation and terms

x: Sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and cemented into successive layers called strata.
Clay contains pore spaces but its very fine particles prevent the easy passage of water; hence it is
porous but impermeable
Chalk and sandstone are porous and permeable, clay is porous but impermeable, whereas
granite
is generally neither porous nor permeable.

secs.t: Metamorphic rocks — parent → metamorphosed rock

x: Limestone -> marble (a-iii), shale/clay -> slate (b-iv), sandstone -> quartzite (c-i), coal -> graphite via anthracite (d-ii).
Garnet, kyanite and sillimanite are typical metamorphic minerals.
Thermal or contact metamorphism and regional or dynamic metamorphism are the broad forms identified in this classification.
Igneous and sedimentary rocks can become metamorphic under heat and pressure.

secs.t: Rock cycle — processes linking the three types

x: Surface rocks undergo weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition; lithification forms sedimentary rocks, heat and pressure form metamorphic rocks, and melting produces magma.
Any rock may enter different pathways in the rock cycle, and exposed metamorphic rocks can weather into sediment.
Carbon dioxide in rainwater forms
carbonic acid
, which helps weather rocks.

secs.t: Persons, institutions and terms of rock study

x: Lithology describes the physical character of a rock unit, particularly its texture, grain size and composition.
Giovanni Arduino developed the geological time scale in 1760, the Standard time scale was set in Italy in 1881, and the Indian time scale was advocated by Sir T.H. Holland.
Uranium dating
is used to determine the age of very old materials.

secs.t: Rock systems of India → age, rocks and resources

x: The Dharwar system contains high-grade
iron ore, manganese, copper, lead and gold
and is economically the most important system.
The Tertiary (Eocene-Pliocene, ~60-7 million years) holds Himalayan sediments, Karewas, Bhangar and Khadar, saw the birth of the Himalayas, and holds the petroleum of Assam and Gujarat.
The Cuddapah system (Purana, ~1,400-600 million years) is sedimentary - shale, slate, quartzite and limestone; shales and slates are clay rocks, so the key was 'clay'.

secs.t: Rocks of AP → districts and resources

x: Khondalites and charnockites are Archaean rocks, more than 2.5 billion years old, and are associated with the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt.
Gondwana is associated with coal, Deccan Trap patches consist of basalt linked with black cotton soil, the KG basin has marine sediments, and the Cuddapah basin is Proterozoic sedimentary.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh is called ‘Ratna Garbha’ because of its
mineral wealth
Enhanced rock weathering involves spreading crushed basalt on farmland; weathering can lock carbon dioxide as bicarbonate.
Kadapa-Kurnool limestone supports the cement industry, Eastern Ghats mining requires social and ecological safeguards, and gold mining is reviving at Ramagiri in the Dharwar greenstone belt.

rows.title: Earth movements - continental drift, sea-floor spreading, plate tectonics and plate boundaries
sub: Group-II S2-5: Plate tectonics, continental drift, folding and faulting

secs.t: Theories → proponents, year and mechanism

x: All three statements correctly describe Holmes’s convection-current mechanism: radioactive heat drives convection, rising limbs split crust at ridges, and sinking limbs drag plates toward trenches.
Harry Hess
proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s, including the creation of new crust at mid-ocean ridges and its destruction at trenches.

secs.t: Pangaea and its parts — terms → present landmasses

x: Gondwanaland included South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar and Arabia.
Laurasia was the northern unit and included Asia minus India.

secs.t: Evidences — continental drift and sea-floor spreading

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2025 counted rock belts, placer gold and a third evidence as ALL correct.
The Ghana coast has placer gold but lacks the corresponding source rock; the source is located in the Brazil plateau, suggesting former continental continuity.
Vine and Matthews
explained the symmetrical magnetic stripes as evidence supporting sea-floor spreading in 1963.

secs.t: Plates → location and monitoring

x: Nazca is a minor plate.
The Philippine Plate lies between the Asiatic and Pacific plates.
The Caribbean Plate borders the South American Plate, and Venezuela lies on this boundary.
Plate movement is monitored using
GPS data

secs.t: Plate boundaries → motion and examples

x: The Red Sea and East African Rift are divergent settings associated with the separation of the Nubian, Somalian and Arabian plates near the Afar triple junction.
Earthquakes occur at all three major boundary types: through stretching at divergent boundaries, subduction-related friction at convergent boundaries, and sudden slip at transform boundaries.

secs.t: India in Gondwanaland and the Indian plate — drift, collision, new findings

x: The Deccan Traps erupted as the northward-moving Indian Plate crossed near the equator and passed over the Reunion hotspot.
Delamination refers to the denser lower layer of the plate peeling away and sinking into the mantle at approximately 100 kilometres depth.
The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through
northward subduction of the Neo-Tethys Plate
and lies between the Indus and Shyok suture zones.

secs.t: Folding and fold mountains — terms and examples

x: The Alps are young fold mountains of Europe; the Appalachians are old fold mountains of North America; the Rockies are young fold mountains of North America; and the Urals are old fold mountains along the Europe–Asia divide.
The Himalayas formed from Tethyan sediments, experienced uplift during the stated epochs, began forming about 70 million years ago, continue to rise, and include the youngest Siwalik range.

secs.t: Faults → force, movement and places

x: A normal fault has a downward-moving hanging wall; a reverse fault has an upward-moving hanging wall; a thrust fault is a low-angle reverse fault; and a strike-slip fault involves horizontal movement due to shear.
Satpura is a block mountain, the Narmada and Tapi occupy rift valleys, and the Vosges and Rhine Valley represent horst and graben features respectively.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The observed rapid episode of sinking, spreading and lava emplacement suggested that sea-floor spreading can occur in bursts rather than at a uniform rate.
Plate movement helps explain mountains, earthquakes, volcanoes and even long-term climate change.
The Eastern Ghats are old, highly eroded and discontinuous hills of the stable Gondwana shield.

rows.title: Folding, faulting, mountain building; isostasy

secs.t: Diastrophism — definition and types

x: Orogenic movements are mountain-building movements caused mainly by horizontal or tangential forces and involve folding and faulting in narrow belts.
Diastrophism includes crustal movements that move, raise or build up the crust, including earthquakes and plate movements.
The Peninsular Block largely escaped folding but experienced vertical movements such as transgression and regression, representing an
epeirogenic effect

secs.t: Scholars → mountain-building and isostasy theories

x: Isostasy refers to the gravitational balance of crustal blocks floating on denser underlying material.
Airy’s model explains relief through variations in crustal thickness at broadly uniform density, with mountains having deep roots.
The sequence is lithogenesis, involving sedimentation; orogenesis, involving folding and mountain building; and gliptogenesis, involving uplift and denudation.

secs.t: Folds — terms → meaning

x: Isoclinal limbs are parallel, an overturned limb passes beyond the vertical, a recumbent fold is nearly horizontal, and a nappe is a strongly displaced recumbent fold.
The Siwaliks display simple anticline–syncline folds of the Jura type.

secs.t: Mountain types → examples; fold mountains by age

x: Exam angle: APPSC G2 2024 - of Appalachians, Aravallis, Alps, Urals, only the
Alps
are young fold mountains.
Fujiyama, Etna and Kilimanjaro are volcanic mountains; the Eastern Ghats are residual mountains; and the Black Forest is a block mountain.
Young fold mountains such as the Himalayas and Alps have
rugged relief and high conical peaks

secs.t: Block mountains and rift valleys — horst, graben → location

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2024 - "Vosges - Central Asia - fold" and "Alps - block" are wrong pairs; Appalachians (fold, N. America) and Andes (fold, S. America) are right.
The Vosges in France and the Black Forest in Germany are horsts flanking the Rhine rift valley, which is a graben.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court accepted the uniform definitions and paused new mining leases in November 2025, while the MoEF&CC ordered a complete ban on new leases on 24 December 2025.
Collapsing hanging glaciers in high-seismicity Himalayan zones can trigger GLOFs and landslide-lake outburst floods.
The Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh are old, heavily eroded residual hills and form part of the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt.

rows.title: Volcanoes - types, materials, landforms, global distribution

secs.t: Volcano terms → meaning — anatomy, lava, pyroclasts, gases, instruments

x: A caldera is a cauldron-shaped depression formed when a large eruption empties the magma chamber and the summit collapses.
Acidic or felsic lava is silica-rich and viscous, making eruptions more explosive.
Pyroclastic flows and lahars, or volcanic mudflows, are associated particularly with
stratovolcanoes
Water vapour is the most abundant volcanic gas, followed by CO2 and SO2.

secs.t: Volcano types — by activity and by form → examples

x: Shield volcanoes are broad and have gentle slopes because they are built by relatively fluid basaltic lava.
Hayli Gubbi in Ethiopia is identified as a
shield volcano
Composite or stratovolcanoes are steep, consist of alternating lava and ash layers, and are associated with explosive eruptions.
A
cinder cone
is a small, steep cone made of loose pyroclasts.

secs.t: Volcano locations — world belts and hot springs → state

x: Basaltic lava plateaus such as the Deccan weather to form
fertile black soil
Manikaran is a hot spring and geothermal site in the Kullu Valley of Himachal Pradesh.
Puga Valley and Chumathang are geothermal sites in
Ladakh
The
Pacific Ring of Fire
has the greatest concentration of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes.

secs.t: India → volcanoes and mud volcanoes → location

x: Exam angle: the APPSC GS 2021 key gives "Barren island" for mud volcanoes - the correct answer is
Baratang
; Barren is the magmatic active volcano.
The Deccan Traps are fissure or flood-basalt outpourings on the Maharashtra Plateau that occurred at the end of the Cretaceous and are linked to the Reunion hotspot.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The renewed eruption of Guatemala's Volcan de Fuego is associated with the Cocos Plate subducting beneath the Caribbean Plate.
ONGC drilled India's first and deepest geothermal wells at Puga Valley in Ladakh to a depth of 1,000 metres for a 1 MW pilot project.
Chittoor, Kadapa, Prakasam and Nellore are all associated with the occurrence of igneous granite, dolerite and gabbro.

rows.title: Earthquakes - causes, seismic waves, measurement, distribution, effects
sub: Group-II S2-6: Earthquakes and volcanoes - causes, types, distribution and effects

secs.t: Earthquake terms → meaning — focus, epicentre, depth, seismic doublet

x: Continental mantle earthquakes begin more than 80 km below the Moho, while normal crustal earthquakes generally occur at depths of 10–29 km.
A seismic doublet consists of two independent earthquakes of similar magnitude occurring in quick succession and close together.
The Venezuelan seismic doublet consisted of earthquakes of magnitude 7.1 and 7.5 in quick succession near the Caribbean–South American strike-slip boundary.

secs.t: Causes of earthquakes — type → cause → example

x: The Ring of Fire is associated mainly with volcanic and convergent-margin activity, not with the San Andreas-type transform setting.
The Latur earthquake occurred far from a plate boundary and showed that stable continental regions can experience earthquakes along concealed or old faults.
The Koyna earthquake of 1967 is the classic Indian example of reservoir-induced seismicity, associated with the filling and weight of a large reservoir.

secs.t: Seismic waves → arrival, motion, medium; shadow zone

x: S-waves are transverse (shear motion perpendicular to travel), and their absence beyond about 105° from the epicentre shows the outer core is liquid.
Love and Rayleigh waves move along the Earth's surface and are classified as
surface waves
P-waves are the fastest and arrive first; they are longitudinal (compressional, push-pull) and pass through solids, liquids and gases.

secs.t: Magnitude vs intensity — scales → persons and instruments → use

x: Exam angle: "Richter scale measures intensity" is wrong - it measures
magnitude
; earthquakes still cannot be predicted accurately.
Exam angle: magnitude = energy at the focus; intensity = effect at a place.
An increase of one magnitude unit on the Richter scale represents a tenfold increase in wave amplitude and an approximately 31-fold increase in energy released.
A seismograph records and measures earthquakes; a seismometer is its sensor; a seismoscope only indicates that a tremor occurred and its time; and a tiltmeter measures ground tilt.

secs.t: Seismic belts → plate setting and places

x: The
Circum-Pacific belt
, also called the Ring of Fire, contains the world's greatest concentration of earthquakes and is associated largely with subduction around the Pacific basin.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is linked to subduction, the Mid-Atlantic belt to a divergent ridge, the Mediterranean-Himalayan belt to continental collision, and hotspots to mantle plumes.

secs.t: Major earthquakes → place, year, setting; effects — Major earthquakes

x: The Latur earthquake occurred in an intraplate region that was then classified as low-risk
Zone I
The 2001 Bhuj earthquake contributed to the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the establishment of the National Disaster Management Authority.
The 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal had a magnitude of 7.8, occurred along the Main Himalayan Thrust and caused liquefaction in parts of the Gangetic plain.
Tohoku 2011 (M 9.0) was a Pacific plate subduction quake (tsunami, Fukushima) = iii.

secs.t: Major earthquakes → place, year, setting; effects — Effects → condition / region

x: Seismic seiches are standing waves that may develop in enclosed or partly enclosed water bodies such as rivers, reservoirs and ponds.
A tsunami generally requires an earthquake of magnitude greater than 6.5, a focus shallower than approximately 70 km and vertical uplift of the sea floor.
Earthquakes trigger landslides in the fragile Himalaya and North-East, liquefaction in soft Indo-Gangetic soils, seiches in lakes and reservoirs, and fires through broken gas and power lines.

secs.t: India → seismic zones → states and cities (IS 1893: 2016) — Tectonic setting

x: India lies in the Alpine-Himalayan seismic belt, which extends eastward through the North-East into Myanmar.
The Indian Plate moves northward into the Eurasian Plate at approximately 5 centimetres per year.
In Myanmar, the
Sagaing Fault
marks the continuation of the Indian–Eurasian boundary through the eastern part of the seismic belt.

secs.t: India → seismic zones → states and cities (IS 1893: 2016) — Zones → areas

x: Exam angle: "Which State/UT has no area in Zone V?" Answer: Andhra Pradesh.
Earthquake vulnerability in India is associated with Himalayan and North-Eastern regions, liquefaction-prone alluvial plains, peninsular faults and the Andaman and Nicobar region.
Under the four-zone map in force, Zone II represents low risk, Zone III moderate risk, Zone IV high risk and Zone V very high risk.

secs.t: Seismic codes → year and provision — IS 1893 history, 2025 Zone VI and rollback

x: After the 1993 Latur earthquake, Zone I was merged into
Zone II
, resulting in the four-zone classification under IS 1893:2002.
The 2025 revision introduced a new top Zone VI for parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch, and placed more than 60% of India’s landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
The 2025 revision was withdrawn after MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA objected to the cost implications.

secs.t: Institutes → location — seismic monitoring and warning; FIRSTs

x: The network detects every Indian earthquake of magnitude 3.0 or above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or above, including tsunami-capable events.
The MoES app RISEQ is now called “
Bhookamp
.” IndiaQuake is the public-alert app of the National Centre for Seismology.
The NCS’s
IndiaQuake
app provides public earthquake alerts.
India built its Tsunami Early Warning System after
the 2004 Sumatra earthquake
and tsunami.

secs.t: Volcanoes — products, gases and types → examples

x: Volcanic gases consist mostly of
water vapour
, followed by carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.
Shield volcanoes have
fluid basaltic lava and gentle slopes
Composite or stratovolcanoes have viscous lava, steep cones, explosive activity and constitute approximately 60% of Earth's volcanoes.
Strombolian eruptions involve frequent, mild bursts of bombs and ash, whereas Vulcanian eruptions are more explosive.

secs.t: Volcanic landforms — intrusive form → shape; Ladakh Magmatic Arc

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2024 - "phacoliths are large domed mounds" is the wrong statement; domes are laccoliths.
The Ladakh Magmatic Arc is located in the Trans-Himalaya between the
Indus and Shyok suture zones
The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through subduction of the Neo-Tethys plate beneath Eurasia and experienced a batholith phase from approximately 160 Ma to less than 45 Ma.
Lava plateau
s, cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas and lava flows are extrusive volcanic landforms.

secs.t: World volcanoes → country and status; largest and highest

x: Stromboli gives its name to Strombolian eruptions and exhibits near-continuous activity.
Etna is Europe's largest and most active volcano, is approximately 3,300 m high and has been a UNESCO site since 2013.
Mount
Vesuvius
is an active volcano in Italy and buried Pompeii in AD 79.
Ojos del Salado is in Chile and is the world's highest active volcano, at 6,893 m; it is not dormant.
White Island (Whakaari) is in
New Zealand
and erupted in December 2019.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: An M 7.7 quake struck off Flores Island, Indonesia, on 18 August 2026.
Despite its M 8.8 megathrust magnitude, the Kamchatka earthquake
caused only a limited tsunami
Experts argued that the restored 2016 hazard values were
too low for the Himalaya
About 95% of earthquake deaths occur in poorly built one- to three-storey houses.
The first pillar begins with construction according to IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920, together with retrofitting priority buildings.

rows.title: Weathering, mass wasting and soil formation; denudation and the cycle of erosion

secs.t: Denudation and weathering — process → what happens; weathering landforms

x: Carbonation
occurs when carbon dioxide in rainwater forms carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone and converts carbon into bicarbonate.
Exfoliation domes develop through
onion-like peeling of granite
, commonly associated with weathering and pressure or temperature effects.
Denudation proceeds through weathering, mass wasting or erosion, transportation and finally deposition.
Water
is considered the most powerful agent of denudation, although wind, ice and gravity also contribute.

secs.t: Mass wasting — type → nature; conditions and regions

x: Rockfall is free fall from cliffs (ii); a slide is a coherent mass slipping along a surface (iv); a slump is a rotational slip on a curved surface in weak saturated soil (i); a debris flow is a fast water-soil-rock mix after heavy rain or snowmelt (iii).
Mass wasting is especially common on slopes steeper than 30 degrees, where rocks are weak or fractured and slopes are bare.

secs.t: Geomorphologists → cycle of erosion; peneplain, monadnock, inselberg

x: Davis proposed the sequence of youth, maturity and old age, culminating in a low, almost flat peneplain.
Monadnocks
are resistant residual hills that remain above the nearly level surface of a peneplain in Davis’s model.
Inselbergs are residual island-hills characteristic of arid and semi-arid regions, formed through desert erosion by wind and sheet-wash.

secs.t: Soil-forming factors — active vs passive; AP soil formation

x: Andhra Pradesh soils are influenced by climate, altitude, bedrock composition, rainfall and heat, as well as river silt from the Godavari, Krishna and Pennar.
The parent rocks associated with Andhra Pradesh soils include
granite, gneiss, basalt and sedimentary rocks
The five classical factors are parent material, climate, relief or topography, organisms and time.

secs.t: Soil texture data and soils → climate region; in-situ vs transported

x: Heavy rainfall leaches nutrients from rainforest soils, while the warm, wet conditions cause dead organic matter to decompose rapidly.
Podzol
develops under cold taiga or boreal conifer forests and is generally thin, acidic, strongly leached and humus-poor.
In hot, high-rainfall regions, intense leaching removes silica and lime from laterite and concentrates
iron and aluminium oxides

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Soil biodiversity loss is ranked
fourth
among the seven threats, after erosion, loss of soil organic carbon and nutrient mismanagement.
The study found that steep, glacier-fed Himalayan catchments release CO2 through
pyrite oxidation
Water is identified as the most powerful agent of soil erosion; sheet, rill and gully are forms of water erosion, while wind erosion dominates in the Thar.

src: Sources: APSES 2024-25 p.50; CDI (Block14 AP Geography - Soils of AP; Block05 AP SES 2025-26 Complete Analysis; Block07 Pollution and Erosion; Block06 Landslides); APP (AP Geography > Soils; Indian Geography Part 1 > Soils of India, Peninsular Plateau, Rock Cycle); UPSC (Indian Geography p.119-120; Environment p.26); LENS Jul 2025 p.116, Nov 2025 p.77; LENSD 3 Sep 2026; TH 13 Sep 2026

rows.title: Major landforms - fluvial landforms and river profiles

secs.t: River course → work and features; profile terms → meaning

x: The youthful upper course has a steep gradient and strong vertical erosion, producing V-shaped valleys, gorges, canyons, waterfalls, rapids and potholes.
In stream capture, headward erosion allows one stream to breach the divide of a neighbouring basin and divert the upper course of the captured stream.
Young, rugged Himalayan relief produces sharp drainage divides, whereas prolonged erosion on old plateaus tends to make divides less distinct or faint.

secs.t: Erosional landforms → formation; gorge vs canyon; ravines → region — Landform → formation

x: Rills enlarge into gullies and then valleys through predominantly vertical erosion, producing a V-shaped valley.
When uplift rejuvenates a river, renewed vertical erosion may incise pre-existing meanders deeply into resistant bedrock.
Overland flow first gathers into rills; the rills merge, deepen into gullies, and a dense network of gullies produces badland topography.

secs.t: Erosional landforms → formation; gorge vs canyon; ravines → region — Gorge vs canyon (Grand Canyon)

x: Exam angle: badland region picked from options (Chambal vs Rann of Kutch, Godavari delta, western coastal plain).
The Dihang gorge is associated with the
Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon near Namcha Barwa
, where the Brahmaputra enters India.
The Chos of Hoshiarpur in Punjab are identified as another region of ravine and badland topography besides the Chambal valley.

secs.t: Depositional landforms → formation; meanders and terraces

x: Deposition on the concave side of a meander can steepen and narrow the loop until it is cut off, leaving stagnant water known as an oxbow lake.
The outer, concave bend experiences erosion and forms a cliff, whereas the inner, convex slip-off side receives deposition.
Braided channels, alluvial fans and natural levees
are depositional features.

secs.t: Delta types → river; estuaries; largest delta

x: Heavy sediment load, shallow coastal water, and sufficiently slow and steady flow favour delta formation.
The west-flowing Deccan rivers commonly have steep gradients, hard-rock channels and short courses, conditions that favour estuaries rather than extensive deltas.
An estuary is a partly enclosed river mouth that retains a free connection with the sea and functions as an ecotone.

secs.t: Drainage patterns → rock and place

x: Dendritic
drainage develops over relatively uniform rock and resembles the branching form of a tree; it is characteristic of the northern plains.
Trellis drainage develops in folded terrain, with tributaries commonly joining the main streams at right angles; the Appalachians provide an example.
Rectangular drainage develops where joints and faults guide stream courses, producing frequent right-angle bends, especially on joint-controlled plateaus.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The seven deltas are Ganga-Brahmaputra, Nile, Mekong, Yangtze, Amazon, Irrawaddy and Mississippi.
Excessive groundwater extraction and reduced sediment or silt supply are identified as the main causes of delta sinking.
The major Andhra Pradesh coastal plain is built primarily by the
Godavari and Krishna
deltas; Konaseema is associated with the Godavari delta.

src: Sources: APP (Indian Geography Pt 1 > Fluvial Landforms; Northern Plains; Peninsular Plateau; Brahmaputra System; AP Geography > Coastal Plains); CDI (Block14 Major Landforms AP; Block14 AP Geography updated 26-07-2026); UPSC (Environment p.37; Indian Geography p.20); LENS Jun 2025 p.124; VIS PT365 Apr 2026 Pt 1 p.68; APSES 2024-25 Annexure 5.26

rows.title: Major landforms - glacial, arid/aeolian, karst and coastal landforms
sub: Group-II S2-7: Major landforms and their features - fluvial, glacial, arid, karst and coastal

secs.t: Landform → geomorphic agent; weathering and mass wasting types

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2023 matched Delta - running water, Cirque - glaciers, Cliffs - waves and currents, Sand dunes - winds.
In Andhra Pradesh, weathering of granite and gneiss gives rise to
red soil
s.
Delta, V-valley, gorge and canyon
are formed by running water.
A doline is a solutional depression produced by groundwater action in limestone, not by a glacier.

secs.t: Fluvial landforms → river stage; delta type → condition

x: Gorges commonly form in hard rocks, while canyons form in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks.
The
Brahmaputra
is a classic example of a river with a braided channel, and its sandbars are locally called chars.
The Nile and Sundarbans are examples of arcuate deltas, Tiber represents a cuspate delta, and the Mississippi represents a bird-foot delta.

secs.t: River-plain terms → meaning and region; plain types

x: Bhabar
is the coarse gravel and pebble belt at the foothills where Himalayan rivers enter the plains.
The Terai lies south of the Bhabar and is a marshy, forested belt where streams that disappeared into the Bhabar come back to the surface.
A peneplain is a nearly featureless surface produced by prolonged erosion, and the Peninsular Plateau is described as a
rejuvenated peneplain

secs.t: Glacial landforms → meaning

x: A cirque is the armchair-shaped hollow at the valley head (iii); an arete is the knife-edge ridge between two cirques (i); a horn is the pointed peak formed when cirques cut back from several sides, like the Matterhorn (ii).
An
outwash plain
consists of sand and gravel deposited by meltwater streams issuing from a glacier.

secs.t: Aeolian (arid) landforms → meaning

x: A
deflation hollow
is produced by the wind lifting and removing loose fine particles, leaving a depression.
Wind-driven sand is concentrated near the ground and abrades the base more than the upper part, producing an undercut mushroom rock.
A mesa is a broad, flat-topped table hill; continued erosion may reduce it to a smaller butte.

secs.t: Karst terms → meaning; speleothems; longest caves

x: Karst landscapes are carved mainly by groundwater dissolving
limestone or dolomite
A sinkhole is a small depression; several sinkholes may form a doline, several dolines may merge into a uvala, and a polje is a much larger depression often related to cave collapse.
Krem Liat Prah in Meghalaya is identified as India’s longest natural cave, while Mammoth Cave in the USA is identified as the world’s longest natural cave.

secs.t: Caves and prehistoric sites → location — India and AP — Caves → location → karst or not

x: Belum Caves are developed in black limestone and contain stalactites and stalagmites, reflecting their karst nature.
Robert Bruce Foote is associated with the first discovery of Belum Caves in 1884, while
H. D. Gebauer
mapped them during 1982–84.
Undavalli consists of rock-cut cave temples associated with the Vishnukundins and contains a reclining Anantasayana Vishnu.

secs.t: Caves and prehistoric sites → location — India and AP — Prehistoric sites and geomorphic landmarks → district

x: Kethavaram caves are in Kurnool district, and deer is the most frequently painted animal.
Billa Surgam is associated with Kurnool/Nandyal and not Anantapuramu.

secs.t: Coastal erosion — agents, processes, landforms, defences

x: The usual sequence is cliff and wave-cut platform, sea cave, arch, stack and finally stump.
Harbours, sand mining, offshore dredging and dams can all disturb or reduce the natural supply and movement of coastal sediment.
The east coast is soft, low-lying and largely alluvial, and its flat wide plains allow inland movement of the sea.

secs.t: Coastal deposition terms → meaning; coast type → example

x: Parallel mountain ranges characterise the Dalmatian coast, while ranges at right angles are associated with ria coasts.
A
beach
is the zone of sand or shingle between the low- and high-tide limits.
When a bar closes a bay, the enclosed water body becomes a
lagoon
Norway has fiord coasts, north-western Spain has ria coasts, and the Adriatic coast of Croatia is a Dalmatian coast.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Hanging glaciers are stranded on steep slopes as the main glacier thins.
The
Geological Survey of India
declared Belum Caves a Geo-Heritage Site.
Erra Matti Dibbalu are late-Quaternary red dunes in Visakhapatnam.
From 2025, the Central Water Commission monitors 2,843 glacial lakes and water bodies, including 2,485 glacial lakes; the earlier number was 902.

rows.title: Atmosphere - structure (layers) and composition
sub: Group-II S2-8: Structure and composition of the atmosphere

secs.t: Composition of the atmosphere — gas → % by volume; variable constituents

x: Per the WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin 2025, CO2 rose by 3.5 ppm to
in 2024, the largest rise since 1957 and about 152% of the pre-industrial level.
Dust is concentrated in the lower atmospheric layers and is more abundant in
subtropical and temperate belts
, where dry winds help raise and transport particles.

secs.t: Layers of the atmosphere → height, temperature trend, phenomena — Division by composition

x: The heterosphere is described as having nitrogen, atomic oxygen, helium and hydrogen in upward order according to molecular weight.

secs.t: Layers of the atmosphere → height, temperature trend, phenomena — Division by temperature

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 - meteorites burn up in the
mesosphere
(not thermosphere/ionosphere).
The
stratosphere and thermosphere
are reversal layers in which temperature increases with height, unlike the normal decrease in the troposphere and mesosphere.
Jet aircraft commonly cruise near the base of the stratosphere because the air is relatively calm and free from most clouds and turbulence.

secs.t: Layers of the atmosphere → height, temperature trend, phenomena — Phenomena → layer (quick revision)
Boundaries → height — tropopause, stratopause, mesopause; troposphere thickness

x: In the troposphere, temperature falls by approximately 1°C for every 165 metres, or about 6.5°C per kilometre.
Strong heating at the equator generates powerful convection currents that carry heat upward, making the tropopause higher there.
The temperature at the tropopause is about -80°C over the equator and -45°C over the poles.

secs.t: Ionosphere — layer → height → scientist name; radio communication

x: The ionosphere contains charged particles that reflect radio waves back to Earth, making long-distance communication possible.
Solar flares and geomagnetic storms can disturb ionospheric conditions and disrupt
GNSS signals
The D layer absorbs medium and long waves, the E layer reflects medium-frequency radio waves, and the F layer is the main reflector of short-wave radio.

secs.t: Ozone layer — location, formation cycle, role, unit

x: Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful UV-B and UV-C radiation and thereby acts as a shield for life on Earth.
Increased UV exposure is associated with skin cancer, cataract, immune suppression and reduced crop yield.
Ultraviolet radiation splits O2 into free oxygen atoms; these combine with O2 to form O3, which absorbs UV and can split back into oxygen molecules and atoms.

secs.t: Ozone depletion — ODS → use; halocarbons and the ozone hole

x: Halocarbons such as CFCs and HCFCs release chlorine and bromine atoms that destroy ozone faster than it can form.
The Antarctic ozone hole develops mainly from
August to November
, during the Southern Hemisphere spring, aided by polar stratospheric clouds.
The ozone hole came into focus in 1985; some older accounts cite 1983, but 1985 is the stated reference year here.

secs.t: Ozone treaties → year → provision; India

x: The Montreal Protocol was adopted in 1987 and controls or phases out nearly 100 ozone-depleting substances.
The Kigali Amendment, adopted in Kigali, Rwanda, in 2016, provides for the phase-down of HFCs, which are ozone-safe but have high global-warming potential.
India was the first developing country to phase out HCFC-141b in rigid foam and achieved a 44% reduction against a 35% target by January 2020.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The method maps
the topside ionosphere
over India up to 1,000 km and is intended to improve NavIC and GPS accuracy.
The Antarctic ozone hole in 2025 peaked at just over 21 million square kilometres and closed early.
The atmosphere is relatively transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation, thereby contributing to the greenhouse effect.

rows.title: Insolation and heat budget; horizontal and vertical distribution of temperature, inversion
sub: Group-II S2-9: Insolation, heat budget and the distribution of temperature

secs.t: Insolation — factors and latitudinal distribution; hottest latitudes

x: The angle of the rays, duration of sunshine, atmospheric transparency, and slope and aspect of land all influence insolation.
Vertical rays concentrate solar energy over a smaller area, producing greater heating than oblique rays.
Sub-tropical deserts around 20°–30° N have
clear skies and dry air
, permitting very high temperatures; the Equator does not record the highest temperatures merely because it receives strong insolation.

secs.t: Heating processes → mechanism; vertical distribution and lapse rate

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2023 matched Advection - horizontal, Convection - vertical, Insolation - direct, Conduction - lower layers.
The Loo transfers heat horizontally through moving air and is therefore an example of
advection
Temperature normally falls with height at about
6.5 °C per km
, because the air is heated from below and higher air absorbs less heat.

secs.t: Albedo — surface → albedo data; clouds; ice-albedo feedback

x: Melting ice exposes dark ocean water, which has a lower albedo and absorbs more heat, producing a positive ice-albedo feedback.
The Arctic has warmed by at least 2 deg C and is warming
3-4 times faster
than the global average (older estimates said about twice), driven by the ice-albedo feedback in which melting ice exposes dark ocean.

secs.t: Earth's heat budget — data (NCERT units)

x: Approximately 35 of every 100 units received at the top of the atmosphere are reflected back to space, giving an overall planetary albedo of about
35 percent
Of 100 units, 35 are reflected to space, 14 are absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 are absorbed by the Earth's surface.
27 by clouds, 6 by scattering, 2 by snow/ice.

secs.t: Greenhouse effect — gases → share and source; GWP; warming data

x: Nitrous oxide is associated mainly with fertilisers and the burning of coal or biomass, not ocean tides and volcanic waves.
Water vapour
is the most abundant greenhouse gas and functions importantly as a climate feedback.
On the stated 100-year scale, carbon dioxide has a GWP of 1, methane 28–36 and nitrous oxide 265–298.

secs.t: Horizontal distribution and range of temperature — isotherms, thermal equator, continentality — Isotherms and thermal equator

x: In January, Northern Hemisphere isotherms bend equatorward over colder landmasses and poleward over relatively warmer oceans.
Isotherms connect places of equal temperature, generally follow an east-west direction, and are more regular in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere.
During Indian winter, temperature generally increases from north to south, consistent with the southward decrease in latitude.

secs.t: Horizontal distribution and range of temperature — isotherms, thermal equator, continentality — Range of temperature

x: The maritime influence reduces the coastal diurnal range, whereas the interior Rayalaseema region generally has a higher range.
Clear skies allow greater radiational loss of heat from the Earth, whereas clouds send some outgoing heat back toward the surface.
Continentality
causes large annual and daily temperature ranges in continental interiors, while maritime influence moderates temperature near coasts.

secs.t: Temperature inversion — conditions, types, effects

x: Long winter nights, clear skies, calm and dry air, and snow cover favour rapid surface cooling and inversion formation.
Cold, dense air flows downslope and accumulates in valleys, producing frost pockets while the slopes remain relatively warmer.
Inversions can produce fog, frost and smog and can trap pollutants within the planetary boundary layer.

secs.t: Places → temperature extremes; urban heat islands

x: Concrete and asphalt absorb and retain heat, causing urban areas to be warmer than their rural surroundings.
Dras in Ladakh recorded approximately −45°C in 1908.
Rentachintala in Palnadu is identified as the hottest place, while Lambasingi is the coolest place in Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Heat waves — IMD criteria, guidelines and AP districts

x: The threshold maximum temperatures are 40°C for plains, 37°C for coasts and 30°C for hills.
A departure
above 6.4°C
from the normal temperature constitutes a severe heat wave; 4.5°C to 6.4°C corresponds to a heat wave.
An actual maximum of 45°C or more in the plains is treated as a heat wave on its own, apart from the departure-from-normal criterion.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: TRISHNA is an ISRO-CNES thermal-infrared mission.
A heat dome develops when a high-pressure system stalls beneath a slowed and meandering jet stream, producing persistent heat.
The oceans took up a record +23 zettajoules of heat in 2025 (against +16 ZJ in 2024), about 90% of the excess heat.

rows.title: Atmospheric pressure - pressure belts; planetary, periodic and local winds; jet streams
sub: Group-II S2-10: Atmospheric pressure, planetary and local winds, jet streams

secs.t: Pressure terms → meaning; instruments → what they measure

x: Isobars join places of equal atmospheric pressure, with pressure values reduced to mean sea level for comparison.
The standard mean sea-level pressure is 1013.25 millibars, equivalent to 1013.25 hectopascals.
A falling barometer indicates decreasing pressure and the possibility of cloudy, rainy or stormy weather.
An anemometer measures wind speed, generally in kilometres per hour or knots.

secs.t: Wind controls — Coriolis force (Ferrel's law), friction, geostrophic wind

x: A geostrophic wind is an upper-air wind blowing parallel to isobars when the pressure gradient force and Coriolis force are balanced and friction is negligible.
The Coriolis force, caused by the Earth's rotation, is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles, so the rotation needed for a cyclone cannot develop within about 5° latitude.

secs.t: Pressure belts → latitude and other name; ITCZ and seasonal shift — Belts & names

x: All three statements correctly give the approximate latitudinal locations of the equatorial, subtropical and subpolar pressure belts.
The equatorial low has calm rising air; the subtropical high has sinking dry air; the subpolar low is a meeting zone of westerlies and polar easterlies; and the polar high has cold sinking air.

secs.t: Pressure belts → latitude and other name; ITCZ and seasonal shift — ITCZ and seasonal shift

x: The belts follow the apparent movement of the overhead sun, shifting about 5°–10° north in the NH summer and south in winter.
In winter, the ITCZ moves south of India and high-pressure cells develop over Tibet and Siberia, setting up the
north-east monsoon
The southward shift of the doldrums brings heavy rain to the southern states during the north-east monsoon and contributes to India’s bimodal rainfall pattern.

secs.t: Planetary winds → direction; circulation cells; southern westerlies → latitude

x: Trade winds (easterlies) steer tropical cyclones westward onto east coasts; on reaching higher latitudes the westerlies turn mature cyclones north-east.

The Roaring Forties blow at 40-50° S, the Furious Fifties at 50-60° S and the Shrieking (Screaming) Sixties around 60° S. So 'Roaring Forties — 30-40° S', 'Furious Fifties — 40-50° S' and 'Shrieking Sixties — 50-60° S' are each shifted one band and wrong.

secs.t: Jet streams → position and role; discoverer; polar vortex — Jet streams

x: Jet streams are narrow, high-velocity upper-level winds generally occurring at about
altitude.
The Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet carries western disturbances, withdraws before the monsoon burst and returns in October as the monsoon ends.
Halley proposed his theory in 1686, Ooishi identified jet streams in the 1920s, their wartime significance became widely known during World War II, and the modern monsoon theory dates to 1957.

secs.t: Jet streams → position and role; discoverer; polar vortex — Polar vortex

x: The polar vortex is a year-round cold, low-pressure region, becomes strongest in winter and its anticlockwise circulation confines cold air near the poles.
The tropospheric part of the polar vortex extends up to about 15 km, while its stratospheric part extends from approximately 15 to 50 km.
Weakening by Rossby waves can reverse the winds, split the vortex and allow cold air to move into the mid-latitudes, producing cold spells.

secs.t: Periodic winds — breezes → time and direction; monsoon theories → proponent

x: The modern monsoon theory of 1957 considers the northward shift of the ITCZ together with jet streams, the Tibet Plateau and ENSO.
'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning
season
; the term refers to the seasonal reversal of winds, but the word itself means season, not reversal, storm or ocean.

secs.t: Local winds and storms → region and effect

x: Foehn occurs in the Alps, while Chinook occurs in the Rockies; both are warm, dry descending winds capable of melting snow.
Sirocco originates in the Sahara and moves towards Italy or the Mediterranean; after picking up moisture, it may produce ‘blood rain’.
Leveche is associated with Spain, Brickfielder with south-east Australia, Blizzard with polar regions and North America, and Shamal with Iraq and the Persian Gulf.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Subtropical Westerly Jet carries the disturbances eastward, and they were associated with intensified weather extremes and possible flash floods in Nepal and Tibet.
El Nino was expected to contribute to below-normal southwest monsoon rainfall in Andhra Pradesh, although short and intense low-pressure spells could partly offset the deficiency.
The AP Survey 2025-26 gives the AP coastline as 1,053.07 km, the 3rd longest in India (the earlier figure of 974 km is still used in some chapters).

rows.title: Humidity, evaporation, condensation, clouds and forms of precipitation
sub: Group-II S2-11: Humidity, condensation, clouds and forms of precipitation

secs.t: Humidity terms → meaning; latent heat; AP humidity data

x: Specific humidity (g/kg) is unaffected by volume changes.
Saturation means relative humidity of 100 per cent.
Warm air can hold more water vapour.
Evaporation absorbs latent heat, while condensation releases it.
Water vapour falls with altitude (and with latitude).
Coastal Andhra has high relative humidity of about 70–90 per cent, contributing to a high heat index.

secs.t: Hydrological cycle — processes; hydrometeorology; India water budget data

x: Evapotranspiration, sublimation and groundwater flow are components of the hydrological cycle.
Hydrometeorology studies
the transfer of water and energy between the land surface and the lower atmosphere
, including rainfall, floods and droughts.
India receives about 4,000 BCM of precipitation annually, of which approximately 1,139 BCM is utilisable, including 690 BCM of surface water and 449 BCM of groundwater.

secs.t: Forms of condensation and precipitation → condition

x: Frost
forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C
. Dew is liquid moisture condensed on cool surfaces with a dew point above 0°C.
Clear and calm nights allow surfaces to cool efficiently, while high humidity and long cold nights favour dew or frost formation.
Coloured rain can result when dust or spores mix with raindrops.

secs.t: Clouds → appearance and height; optical phenomena → cause — Cloud → family → appearance → weather

x: Cirrostratus is a thin milky sheet that can produce a halo, while cirrocumulus consists of small globular masses or ripples.
Cumulonimbus clouds have marked vertical development, may reach about 15 km, and commonly have a towering anvil-shaped top.
Cumulonimbus
, the towering vertical cloud with an anvil top, produces thunderstorms, rainstorms, hail and cloudbursts (APPSC 2019).

secs.t: Clouds → appearance and height; optical phenomena → cause — Optical phenomena → cause

x: A sun halo is typically a ring of about 22° produced when sunlight is refracted through millions of hexagonal ice crystals in thin, high cirrostratus clouds.
A corona consists of coloured rings close to the Sun or Moon and is produced by
diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds

secs.t: Precipitation types → mechanism and place; rain shadow; AP rainfall places

x: Cyclonic or frontal precipitation occurs when warm air rises over cold air along fronts or when air rises in a cyclone’s low-pressure centre.
Equatorial and summer-interior afternoon showers are convectional, Western Ghats rainfall is orographic, and Bay of Bengal cyclones produce cyclonic precipitation.
North Coastal Andhra Pradesh receives the highest rainfall, approximately 140–152 cm, due to the South-West monsoon and the orographic effect of the Eastern Ghats.

secs.t: Cloud seeding, acid rain and cloudbursts — chemicals, coiner, thresholds

x: Silver iodide, dry ice and common salt may be used for cloud seeding, and silver iodide resembles ice crystallographically.
Orographic lifting raises moist air over the Himalayas, encouraging the development of towering cumulonimbus clouds capable of producing cloudbursts.
A cloudburst is rainfall of about 100 mm per hour or more over a small area of 20-30 sq km, usually from cumulonimbus clouds.

secs.t: Instruments and isolines → what they measure or join; earliest rain gauge

x: Wet-bulb equals dry-bulb at 100% relative humidity (saturated air, no evaporative cooling), not at zero.
The Mauryan Arthashastra described a state rain gauge whose measurement was expressed in
drona
, approximately 13.2 kg of water.
The Mauryan Arthashastra description predates Korea’s Cheugugi of 1441, which in turn predates Castelli’s rain gauge of 1639.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A waterspout is a funnel extending from a cumulus or cumulonimbus cloud over a water body.
The 16th Finance Commission recommended the addition of
heatwaves and lightning
to the nationally notified disasters.
Andhra Pradesh receives about 966 mm of average annual rainfall, with approximately two-thirds from the South-West monsoon and one-third from the North-East monsoon.

rows.title: Air masses and fronts - classification and associated weather

secs.t: Air masses — meaning, Bergeron code → source region

x: An air mass is a very large body of air with nearly uniform horizontal temperature and humidity, acquired by remaining over a homogeneous source region.
Cold, dense cP and cA air masses build polar anticyclones, which are cold-core highs and strongest near the surface.
Polar anticyclones are associated with
clear skies, fog, frost and sharp night cooling

secs.t: Air mass modification → weather; stability

x: Warm air over a colder surface is cooled from below, becomes stable and gives fog, stratus and drizzle.
Dust and salt act as hygroscopic condensation nuclei, and water vapour may reach up to 4 percent by volume in the humid tropics.
The transport of warm air masses into the Arctic by a meandering jet stream drives
Arctic amplification

secs.t: Fronts → weather; Bjerknes polar front theory — Front types → weather

x: In a cold front, advancing cold air forms a steep wedge and lifts warm air sharply, producing cumulonimbus, heavy short showers, thunder, squalls and a sudden temperature fall.
Arcus clouds form along the leading edge of thunderstorm outflows or cold fronts and mark the boundary between warm and cool air.

secs.t: Fronts → weather; Bjerknes polar front theory — Terms → meaning

x: Frontolysis occurs when a front weakens and dissolves because temperature contrast is lost; frontogenesis involves formation or sharpening through convergence of contrasting air masses.
A warm front brings falling pressure and steady widespread rain, the warm sector brings warmer humid conditions with easing rain, and the cold front is followed by cold clear air.

secs.t: Air masses affecting India — season → source → effect

x: The Himalayan barrier makes north India about
warmer than places on the same latitude during winter.
The winter anticyclonic cell produces
clear skies, light northerly winds, low humidity and a large daily temperature range
The south-west monsoon is produced by moist maritime air from the Indian Ocean, supplied by the low-level Somali Jet.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh experiences the dual influence of the south-west monsoon and the north-east monsoon, the latter involving winter air returning over the Bay of Bengal.
An Antarctic high extending unusually far north brought snow to Chile's Atacama Desert for the first time in over a decade.
A stalled high-pressure heat dome drove
a record early heatwave in Western Europe
